summary:
FireLens Butte is an interactive historical satellite hotspot explorer for Butte County, California. Using NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS observations, it organizes satellite detections into a shared 1-km cell-day metric to make cross-sensor comparisons more understandable.

The application provides a 302-month historical calendar, interactive maps, sensor comparisons, seasonal context, and downloadable CSV and SVG results. Earlier periods without observed VIIRS data are clearly marked as exploratory MODIS-based estimates.

FireLens helps researchers, students, and land managers explore historical hotspot patterns while understanding differences in sensor sensitivity and coverage. It emphasizes scientific transparency rather than presenting satellite detections as unique wildfires or claiming real-time forecasting capabilities.
details:
FireLens Butte — Historical Satellite Hotspot Explorer

Challenge: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
Team: GeoNexus_M
Study area: Butte County, California, USA (GEOID 06007)

The Problem

NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments have recorded thermal hotspots over many years. However, differences in spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, observation timing, and coverage make direct comparisons difficult.

FireLens addresses this problem by organizing historical observations into a common comparison framework and presenting them through an interactive web application.

Our Solution

FireLens is a historical hotspot exploration tool covering 302 months, from November 2000 through December 2025, for Butte County, California.

Users can:

  • Explore monthly hotspot activity through an interactive calendar.
  • Visualize observed activity on a county map.
  • Compare MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Examine historical seasonal patterns and model evaluation results.
  • Identify observed, unavailable, and estimated values.
  • Download CSV datasets and SVG visualizations.
  • Explore the application online or through its offline release.

Data and Scientific Methodology

We use historical NASA FIRMS MODIS Terra/Aqua and VIIRS Suomi NPP hotspot observations, together with official California county-boundary data.

The processing pipeline filters detections to the county, retains source type-0 presumed-vegetation detections, and maps their coordinates to a fixed 1-km grid using the EPSG:3310 projection.

We then count distinct occupied grid-cell days for each sensor. This provides a common reporting unit while avoiding the assumption that every individual satellite detection represents a separate wildfire.

For earlier periods without observed VIIRS data, we use an exploratory MODIS-to-VIIRS statistical regression crosswalk. Observed VIIRS values begin in February 2012, with January 2012 treated as a partial transition month.

Validation and Results

The processing pipeline independently verified county membership and monthly sensor aggregations against preserved source observations.

For the 2024–2025 evaluation period, the regression crosswalk achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of approximately 20.33 cell-days per month against VIIRS observations, compared with 32.00 for unadjusted MODIS. A simpler calendar-month median baseline performed better at approximately 18.96, which we disclose in the application.

A shared spatial grid does not eliminate differences in satellite sensitivity, observation frequency, or coverage. VIIRS is not ground truth for actual wildfires.

The application also highlights known limitations, such as the July 2024 S-NPP observation outages, unvalidated early historical estimates, and heuristic uncertainty bands.

Technology

The scientific processing system uses Python, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Shapely, PyProj, and Matplotlib.

The interactive frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, SVG, and precomputed scientific datasets.

FireLens is publicly deployed through GitHub Pages. The deployed website operates without a continuously running backend or live NASA API requests.

Impact and Future Potential

FireLens provides a reproducible, accessible way for researchers, students, and land managers to examine historical satellite-detected hotspot activity and understand the limitations of comparing observations from different sensors.

The current implementation is a retrospective research and educational prototype for one county. It does not count unique wildfires, estimate burned area, forecast future fires, or provide operational fire warnings.

Future work could expand regional coverage, investigate sensor-specific observation biases, and explore updated satellite data after additional scientific validation.
